clinicalPearls: The major esophageal symptoms are heartburn, regurgitation, chest pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, and globus sensation; the clinical history is central to evaluation (Harrison 22e p.2503).

Dysphagia for both liquids and solids suggests a motility disorder such as achalasia, whereas dysphagia for solids alone suggests a structural lesion (stricture, web, ring, or tumor) (Harrison 22e p.2504).
Patient localization of where food 'hangs up' is notoriously imprecise; about 30% of distal esophageal obstructions are perceived as cervical (neck) dysphagia (Harrison 22e p.2504).

Intermittent solid-food dysphagia that is unchanged or slowly progressive over years points to a benign process (Schatzki ring or eosinophilic esophagitis), whereas dysphagia progressing over weeks to months raises concern for neoplasia (Harrison 22e p.295).
Odynophagia is uncommon with reflux esophagitis; its presence should raise suspicion of an alternative etiology, particularly pill-induced or infectious esophagitis (Harrison 22e p.2505, p.2513).

Achalasia is diagnosed by barium swallow and/or esophageal manometry; the barium study shows a dilated esophagus with poor emptying, an air-fluid level, and a tapered 'beak-like' narrowing at the LES (Harrison 22e p.2507).

Manometric hallmarks of achalasia are impaired (incomplete) deglutitive LES relaxation plus absent peristalsis; manometry is the most sensitive test as it detects disease before esophageal dilatation (Harrison 22e p.2507-2508).

Endoscopy is a necessary part of the achalasia evaluation to exclude pseudoachalasia from tumor infiltration at the cardia/distal esophagus, which accounts for up to 5% of suspected cases (Harrison 22e p.2507).
The GERD injury spectrum progresses from esophagitis to stricture to Barrett metaplasia to adenocarcinoma; esophageal adenocarcinoma incidence is rising in parallel with GERD (Harrison 22e p.2509).
Erosive esophagitis at the esophagogastric junction is the endoscopic hallmark of GERD but is found in only about one-third of GERD patients (Harrison 22e p.2510).
Eosinophilic esophagitis should be strongly considered in children and adults presenting with dysphagia and food impaction, especially with an atopic history (Harrison 22e p.2511).
EoE is confirmed histologically by esophageal mucosal eosinophilia with a peak density of 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, in the setting of esophageal symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2512).
harrison.pathophysiology: The esophagus is a muscular tube with a sphincter at each end (UES, LES) that transports food and otherwise remains empty. Disease manifests as impaired function (swallowing disorders, excessive gastroesophageal reflux) or pain. Dysphagia is subclassified by mechanism: structural/mechanical narrowing (lumen <13 mm reliably causes solid-food dysphagia) versus propulsive/motor disorders of peristalsis and deglutitive inhibition. In achalasia, autoimmune-mediated loss of myenteric plexus ganglion cells (involving both excitatory cholinergic and inhibitory nitric-oxide neurons), linked to latent HSV-1 infection plus genetic susceptibility, produces impaired deglutitive LES relaxation and absent peristalsis. GERD results from excessive reflux of gastric acid and pepsin causing a cytokine-mediated (rather than directly caustic) inflammatory mucosal injury; pathologic reflux follows progressive distortion of esophagogastric junction architecture (hiatus widening, loss of intraabdominal esophageal segment/flap valve, axial hiatal hernia, increased junction compliance) compounded by impaired acid clearance from disrupted peristalsis or reduced salivation. Eosinophilic esophagitis is an immunologic disorder driven by antigen (chiefly food allergen) sensitization in susceptible individuals, with eosinophil-predominant inflammation. (Harrison 22e p.2503, p.2506-2510, p.2511)
additionalDifferentials: Scleroderma esophagus (absent contractility with weak LES)
Pseudoachalasia from tumor infiltration of the cardia/distal esophagus
Schatzki ring and esophageal webs (Plummer-Vinson/Paterson-Kelly syndrome)
Coronary artery disease (for esophageal-type chest pain)
Functional heartburn / disorders of gut-brain interaction
infectionMimics: Candida esophagitis (white plaques/exudate; C. albicans most common; associated with stasis and immunosuppression)
Herpes simplex virus esophagitis (vesicles and small superficial ulcers; coexisting nose/lip vesicles)
Cytomegalovirus esophagitis (large serpiginous distal ulcers in immunocompromised hosts)
Acute HIV seroconversion esophageal ulceration (with oral ulcers and maculopapular rash)
Tuberculosis or histoplasmosis causing traction midesophageal diverticula
nonInfectiousMimics: Coronary artery disease / angina mimicking esophageal chest pain
Pill esophagitis (singular deep ulcer at points of luminal narrowing, often near the carina, sparing distal esophagus)
Mucocutaneous diseases involving the esophagus (pemphigoid, lichen planus, epidermolysis bullosa)
additionalInvestigations: Upper endoscopy (EGD) - single most useful test for esophageal dysphagia; allows biopsy and dilation
Barium contrast radiography / video fluoroscopic swallow study (better for proximal/cricopharyngeal lesions and esophageal function; 13-mm barium tablet increases stricture detection)
Esophageal high-resolution manometry / pressure topography (diagnose achalasia and DES; assess peristalsis before antireflux surgery)
Functional lumen imaging probe (FLIP) panometry (can evaluate esophageal dysphagia in lieu of manometry; strong correlation for achalasia and normal contractility)
Ambulatory 24-96 h esophageal pH monitoring (pH <4 for >6% of the day indicates GERD), optionally with intraluminal impedance for nonacidic reflux
Esophageal mucosal biopsies (required to distinguish infectious vs eosinophilic vs reflux esophagitis; peak >=15 eosinophils/HPF for EoE)
Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) for staging esophageal cancer and assessing Barrett dysplasia / submucosal lesions
CT scanning when pseudoachalasia is suspected and endoscopy nondiagnostic
redFlags: Progressive solid-food dysphagia with weight loss - classic presentation of esophageal cancer; warrants prompt endoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2507).
Odynophagia (painful swallowing) - usually indicates ulceration; raises suspicion of pill-induced or infectious esophagitis (Harrison 22e p.295, p.2513).
Iron-deficiency anemia / chronic occult GI bleeding accompanying esophageal symptoms.
Hoarseness developing after dysphagia - may indicate recurrent laryngeal nerve compromise by malignancy (Harrison 22e p.295).
Abrupt onset of symptoms (<1 year), advanced age, and weight loss in apparent achalasia - suggests pseudoachalasia from malignancy (Harrison 22e p.2507).
Food impaction with inability to pass a bolus even with liquids - typical of structural dysphagia (Harrison 22e p.295).
Severe cough with swallowing - may signal tracheoesophageal fistula.
Finding of high-grade dysplasia in Barrett esophagus - high rate of progression to and coexisting prevalence of adenocarcinoma; mandates intervention (Harrison 22e p.2511).
harrison.prognosis: Esophageal cancer carries poor survival even when small because abundant esophageal lymphatics permit early regional nodal metastasis. Barrett metaplasia progresses to adenocarcinoma at an estimated 0.1-0.3% per year through low- and high-grade dysplasia, with greatest risk in obese white males in the sixth decade. Untreated achalasia predisposes to stasis esophagitis and increases squamous cell cancer risk roughly 17-fold; durable therapies (pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy, POEM) achieve symptom relief in about 80-90% of patients, though peristalsis does not recover and chest pain responds less well than dysphagia. EoE is chronic with nearly universal recurrence on stopping therapy, requiring maintenance treatment. Erosive esophagitis and peptic strictures have become increasingly rare in the era of potent acid suppression. (Harrison 22e p.2507-2508, p.2510-2512)
pitfalls: Treating presumed GERD empirically without recognizing that persistent dysphagia or chest pain may instead reflect eosinophilic esophagitis, peptic stricture, motility disorder, esophageal cancer, or coronary artery disease (Harrison 22e p.2510).
Attributing 'heartburn' to GERD when the term is misused for indigestion or other sensations - clarify the patient's meaning (Harrison 22e p.2503).
Assuming neck-localized dysphagia is oropharyngeal - about 30% of distal esophageal lesions refer pain proximally (Harrison 22e p.2504).
Mistaking pseudoachalasia (tumor infiltration, up to 5% of cases) for primary achalasia - omit endoscopy at peril (Harrison 22e p.2507).
Diagnosing distal esophageal spasm before excluding the more common peptic and infectious esophagitis and, above all, cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.2509).
Aggressive esophageal dilation in EoE - the stiff-walled esophagus risks deep mural laceration or perforation (Harrison 22e p.2512).
Relying on peripheral blood eosinophilia (present in only 25-50%) or allergy testing (poor sensitivity/specificity) to diagnose EoE or identify trigger foods (Harrison 22e p.2512).

Over-interpreting nonspecific minor manometric findings (hypertensive/hypotensive peristalsis) as a defined motility disorder; reflux and anxiety/depression are common in these patients (Harrison 22e p.2509).
harrison.severityClassification: GERD esophageal injury spectrum (Fig. 334-9): esophagitis -> stricture -> Barrett metaplasia -> adenocarcinoma; reflux testing defines GERD as esophageal pH <4 for >6% of the day. Barrett progression staged histologically as no dysplasia -> low-grade dysplasia -> high-grade dysplasia -> adenocarcinoma. High-resolution manometry differentiates three achalasia subtypes: type I classic (minimal esophageal-body pressurization), type II with esophageal compression/pressurization, and type III spastic achalasia (Fig. 334-6). EoE histologic threshold: peak >=15 eosinophils per high-power field. (Harrison 22e p.2508-2511)
references: Shaheen NJ et al. ACG guideline: diagnosis and management of Barrett's esophagus. Am J Gastroenterol 117:1177, 2022 (Harrison 22e p.2503 Further Reading)
